title: Market Games for Generative Models: Equilibria, Welfare, and Strategic Entry
claim: A multi-layer ecosystem of providers, intermediaries and heterogeneous users defines a market game, raising questions about training, platform choice and welfare.
layout: 3 stacked colored layers with upward arrows, question callouts on right
description: Three horizontal colored bands are stacked vertically. The top orange band is labeled Model Provider and holds three network-graph icons for models g1, g2 and gM. The middle green band is labeled Platform Player and holds icons of a browser window, a laptop with a gear, and stacked windows, indexed 1, 2 and N. The bottom red band is labeled User Group and shows four people icons, θ1 to θK. Black arrows run upward from users to platforms and from platforms to models. Left-side captions read 'Choose g depending on Utility' and 'Choose depending on Score'. On the right, three speech-box callouts pose questions: how to train a new best-response model, how platforms choose models and what happens in a market, and what the effect on social welfare is. The eye goes first to the colored layers.
caption: The three-layer model-platform-user market structure. Model providers develop generative models, platforms select models to deploy, and heterogeneous users choose platforms.
abstract: Generative model ecosystems increasingly operate as competitive multi-platform markets, where platforms strategically select models from a shared pool and users with heterogeneous preferences choose among them. Understanding how platforms interact, when market equilibria exist, how outcomes are shaped by model-providers, platforms, and user behavior, and how social welfare is affected is critical for fostering a beneficial market environment. In this paper, we formalize a three-layer model-platform-user market game and identify conditions for the existence of pure Nash equilibrium. Our analysis shows that market structure, whether platforms converge on similar models or differentiate by selecting distinct ones, depends not only on models' global average performance but also on their localized attraction to user groups. We further examine welfare outcomes and show that expanding the model pool does not necessarily increase user welfare or market diversity. Finally, we design novel best-response training schemes that allow model providers to strategically introduce new models into competitive markets.
